clinicalPearls: Predominantly affects young boys and is usually unilateral, often presenting with leukocoria, strabismus or reduced vision detected incidentally or by a parent
Hallmark findings are retinal telangiectasia and aneurysmal (light-bulb) vessel dilatation with massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid (yellow exudate)
Exudation can progress to an exudative (non-rhegmatogenous) retinal detachment, which in advanced cases fills much of the vitreous cavity
A key differential is retinoblastoma, and distinguishing the two is critical because management and prognosis differ radically
Fluorescein angiography highlights the telangiectatic and aneurysmal vessels, areas of capillary non-perfusion and leakage
Management principles centre on ablating abnormal vessels with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, with anti-VEGF or steroid adjuncts and surgery for advanced detachment
The condition is typically sporadic and non-hereditary, though somatic mutations affecting retinal vascular development are implicated
Early detection and treatment give the best chance of preserving vision and avoiding enucleation for a blind painful eye
reference.pathophysiology: Coats disease is an idiopathic disorder of retinal vascular development in which the retinal capillaries, arterioles and venules become telangiectatic and form saccular aneurysms. Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier in these abnormal vessels allows lipid-rich plasma to leak into and beneath the retina, producing the characteristic yellowish exudate. Progressive exudation and fluid accumulation lead to an exudative retinal detachment, and long-standing disease can cause neovascular glaucoma, cataract and a blind, painful eye. The process is usually unilateral and sporadic, reflecting a localised abnormality of retinal endothelial integrity rather than a systemic vascular disease.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination, often under anaesthesia in children, to map telangiectasia, exudate and detachment
Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate aneurysmal vessels, non-perfusion and leakage
B-scan ultrasonography to assess detachment and exclude the calcification typical of retinoblastoma
Optical coherence tomography to evaluate macular exudate and subretinal fluid where media permit
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) when retinoblastoma cannot be excluded clinically
Wide-field retinal imaging to document extent and monitor treatment response
redFlags: Leukocoria in a child, which mandates urgent exclusion of retinoblastoma
Total exudative retinal detachment threatening irreversible visual loss
Neovascular glaucoma producing a painful blind eye
Rapid progression of exudation despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the stage at diagnosis: eyes treated before macular involvement or extensive detachment can retain useful vision, whereas advanced disease with total detachment or neovascular glaucoma often results in poor vision and may require removal of a painful blind eye.
pitfalls: Mistaking Coats disease for retinoblastoma or vice versa, with catastrophic consequences for management
Underestimating the extent of peripheral telangiectasia and undertreating abnormal vessels
Delaying examination under anaesthesia in an uncooperative child, allowing progression
Failing to monitor for recurrence of exudation after apparently successful ablation
management: Ablation of the telangiectatic and aneurysmal retinal vessels with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy is the mainstay of treatment.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid injections as adjuncts to reduce exudation and subretinal fluid.
Vitreoretinal surgery, such as scleral buckling, subretinal fluid drainage or vitrectomy, for advanced exudative retinal detachment.
Careful exclusion of retinoblastoma before treatment, since management and prognosis differ radically.
Enucleation for a blind, painful eye with neovascular glaucoma.
Amblyopia management and visual rehabilitation in affected children.
Regular monitoring with examination under anaesthesia and wide-field retinal imaging to document extent and treatment response.
